entries.question: Alec controls [Elspeth Conquers Death] and puts the third lore counter it. With the triggered ability, they target [Eternal Witness] in their graveyard. When Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield, can it target Elspeth Conquers Death with its trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the same: Elspeth is sacrificed by state-based actions before Eternal Witness's triggered ability is put on the stack, so that ability can target Elspeth Conquers Death in the graveyard.
entries.answer:
Yes. Elspeth Conquers Death is sacrificed as soon as its chapter III ability leaves the stack (i.e., right after it finishes resolving and returns Eternal Witness), and that sacrifice is a state-based action that doesn't use the stack [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #11]. Eternal Witness's enter trigger isn't put on the stack (and its target isn't chosen) until the next time a player would receive priority, which is after that sacrifice has already happened. So by the time you choose a target, Elspeth Conquers Death is a card in your graveyard and is a legal target for "return target card from your graveyard to your hand."

This mirrors the note that Eternal Witness's ability can target a card that reached your graveyard as the spell/ability putting Eternal Witness onto the battlefield was resolving [Eternal Witness ruling #0].

Timing note: if instead something caused Elspeth Conquers Death to remain on the battlefield (for example, its lore counters were removed before the chapter ability left the stack [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #5]), it would not be in the graveyard and could not be targeted. Nothing here differs between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

When the final chapter ability resolves, Eternal Witness is returned to the battlefield. However, its triggered ability is not put onto the stack until after state based actions are checked. When state based actions are checked, Elspeth Conquers Death is sacrificed because is has a number of lore counters greater than or equal to its final chapter number. After this, triggers are placed onto the stack, and Elspeth Conquers Death is in the graveyard able to be the target of Eternal Witness's triggered ability.

entries.question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Robber of the Rich’s permission to spend mana as though it were any color lets Autumn pay Light Up the Stage’s {R} spectacle cost with {C}.
entries.answer:
Yes — Autumn can pay Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost of {R} using colorless mana, because Robber of the Rich says "During any turn you attacked with a Rogue, you may cast that card and you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." That permission lets Autumn spend {C} as though it were red mana, so a single {C} satisfies the {R} spectacle cost. This card text overrides the general principle that {C} is never interchangeable with a colored symbol.

Conditions that still must be met:
- Autumn attacked with a Rogue this turn. Robber of the Rich is itself a Human Archer Rogue, so attacking with it satisfies that, and the permission works even if Robber of the Rich has since left combat or the battlefield [Robber of the Rich ruling #3][Robber of the Rich ruling #5].
- Spectacle requires that an opponent lost life this turn; it only cares that life was lost, not that the total is still lower [Light Up the Stage ruling #6][Light Up the Stage ruling #7]. Note it's an alternative cost, and any cost increases/reductions apply on top of it [Light Up the Stage ruling #5].
- Neither Robber of the Rich nor spectacle changes when the spell can be cast. Light Up the Stage is a sorcery, so Autumn can only cast it during their own main phase with an empty stack [Robber of the Rich ruling #6][Light Up the Stage ruling #8].
- Casting it removes it from exile; it can't be cast again [Robber of the Rich ruling #8].

Multiplayer note: the answer is the same with more than two players. Nehemiah is simply whoever was the defending player when Robber of the Rich attacked (the planeswalker's controller if it attacked a planeswalker) [Robber of the Rich ruling #9]. Spectacle can even be enabled by an opponent who lost life and later left the game [Light Up the Stage ruling #3], but if Autumn leaves the game, cards Autumn controls via Robber of the Rich's effect are exiled [Robber of the Rich ruling #0].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

Robber of the Rich allows Autumn to cast the card and "may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." This changes how the player may pay a cost, and they can do so with any mana, regardless of color. 

"Spectacle" is an alternative cost ([702.137a]), and can only be used if no other alternative cost is being paid. Luckily, Robber of the Rich does not create an alternative cost, it just changes how mana may be spent.

entries.question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Urza's Saga isn't sacrificed while Jinx's effect applies (it claims it's no longer a Saga), but the reference states it loses its chapter abilities and is immediately sacrificed, so the final rulings disagree.
entries.answer:
Short answer: Urza's Saga becomes the basic land type Alexzander chooses (e.g., an Island) until end of turn. Because it's no longer a Saga while Jinx's effect applies, the "sacrifice after the final chapter" rule doesn't kick in, so Urza's Saga isn't sacrificed — Nico keeps the permanent, and the two lore counters stay on it (nothing removes counters). When Jinx's effect wears off at end of turn, it's an Urza's Saga again with two lore counters, and it will get its third lore counter after Nico's next draw step, at which point chapter III resolves and it's then sacrificed.

Details and caveats:
- Jinx's effect is a type-changing effect applied in layer 4 (see [613.6] for how layers apply). Changing a land to a basic land type replaces its subtypes, which is why the Urza's Saga subtype — and with it the chapter abilities — is gone for the turn.
- [Urza's Saga ruling #1] is the key comparison: a Saga that loses all its chapter abilities but is still a Saga is immediately sacrificed. Here it isn't a Saga at all during Jinx's effect, so that doesn't apply. [Urza's Saga ruling #4] confirms sacrifice happens only after the last chapter ability resolves.
- Abilities Urza's Saga already gained from chapters I and II ({T}: Add {C}, and {2}, {T}: create the Construct token) are retained for as long as it's on the battlefield per [Urza's Saga ruling #5]; those were granted by resolved abilities, not by its subtype.
- Not covered by the rules text you gave me: the exact rule for basic-land-type changes overwriting subtypes and intrinsic abilities (the 305.7 area), and the state-trigger rule for sacrificing a Saga with lore counters ≥ its final chapter number. Those specifics come from the rulings above rather than numbered rules in this context, so treat the "loses chapter abilities, keeps gained abilities" part as grounded in the rulings.
- Nothing here depends on the number of players: the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
In layer 4, Urza's Saga will have its land type overwritten as well as lose all of its chapter abilities. It will gain the abilities to tap for {C} and to create Construct tokens in layer 6, as those abilities are granted by a continuous effect that was generated when the previous chapter abilities resolved..

Because Urza's Saga has lost all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed the next time state-based actions are checked, per the Urza's Saga ruling "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed".

entries.question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude suspending isn't casting so it doesn't count toward Ethersworn Canonist's one-nonartifact-per-turn limit, allowing Ada to suspend Shade of Trokair and then cast Divination (with the candidate correctly noting order and the later cast-from-suspend interaction).
entries.answer:
Yes. Suspending Shade of Trokair is not casting it, so it doesn't use up Ada's one nonartifact spell for the turn, and Divination can then be cast (assuming Ada hasn't cast any other nonartifact spell this turn).

Why: Exiling a card with suspend isn't casting that card — it doesn't even use the stack and can't be responded to [Shade of Trokair ruling #7]. Ethersworn Canonist only cares about nonartifact spells a player has *cast* ("Each player who has cast a nonartifact spell this turn can't cast additional nonartifact spells"), and each player may cast any number of artifact spells plus at most one nonartifact spell per turn [Ethersworn Canonist ruling #1]. Since the suspend action isn't a cast, Ada is still at zero nonartifact spells cast, and Divination (a sorcery, i.e., nonartifact) is that one allowed nonartifact spell.

Two cautions:
1. Order matters. You may exile a card with suspend only at a time when you could cast that card, taking into account effects that stop you from casting it [Shade of Trokair ruling #2]. So if Ada cast Divination first, Ethersworn Canonist would then prevent Ada from casting Shade of Trokair, and therefore Ada could no longer suspend it that turn. Suspend first, then cast Divination — exactly the order asked about — works.
2. Later, when the last time counter is removed and suspend's third ability lets Ada cast Shade of Trokair, that *is* casting a nonartifact spell. If Ethersworn Canonist is still on the battlefield and Ada has already cast a nonartifact spell that turn, Ada can't cast it then; it stays exiled with no time counters and is no longer suspended [Shade of Trokair ruling #5].

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games — Ethersworn Canonist's restriction applies per player independently.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Suspending a card is not casting a spell, so it does not count towards Ethersworn Canonist's restriction.

entries.question: Asa controls an [Inventors' Fair], a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], and two [Piston Sledge]. They want to activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and sacrifice a Piston Sledge to help pay the cost. Is this legal?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that activating Inventors' Fair is legal and you may sacrifice a Piston Sledge to Krark‑Clan Ironworks to produce mana to help pay the cost because the artifact-count legality is checked before mana abilities are activated.
entries.answer:
Yes — this works, with one clarification: sacrificing a Piston Sledge is not part of Inventors' Fair's cost. Inventors' Fair's last ability costs {4}, {T}, and Sacrifice Inventors' Fair. The way a Piston Sledge "helps pay" is by being sacrificed to Krark-Clan Ironworks ("Sacrifice an artifact: Add {C}{C}"), producing {C}{C} that can be applied toward the {4}. The {4} is generic mana, so colorless {C} mana pays it fine (you'd still need two more mana from somewhere for the remaining {2}).

The activation restriction "Activate only if you control three or more artifacts" is satisfied: Inventors' Fair itself is a Legendary Land, not an artifact, but Krark-Clan Ironworks plus the two Piston Sledge are three artifacts. Per [Inventors' Fair ruling #2], the number of artifacts you control is checked only as you activate the ability and is not checked again as it resolves — so dropping to two artifacts by sacrificing a Piston Sledge to Krark-Clan Ironworks while paying costs, or afterward, does not make the ability illegal or cause it to be countered. When it resolves you still search your library for an artifact card, reveal it, put it into your hand, and shuffle.

One timing note: I'm assuming you announce the Inventors' Fair ability first (locking in the artifact-count check), then activate Krark-Clan Ironworks as a mana ability while paying. If instead you sacrifice Piston Sledge to Krark-Clan Ironworks *before* announcing Inventors' Fair's ability, you'd only control two artifacts at the moment of activation and the ability could not legally be activated at all.

Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The process for activating an ability is the same as the process for casting a spell. It must be legal to activate the ability in order to put it onto the stack. Mana abilities are only activated after the legality of activating the original ability has been checked.

entries.question: Amare controls [Psychogenic Probe] and casts [Pain], targeting Nico. They discard a [Progenitus]. Does Psychogenic Probe trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line: Progenitus's replacement causes a reveal-and-shuffle instead of a discard, so Pain still causes the shuffle and Psychogenic Probe triggers, dealing 2 damage to the player who shuffled.
entries.answer:
Yes — Psychogenic Probe triggers, and it deals 2 damage to the player who shuffled, i.e. Nico (assuming Nico is the owner of the discarded Progenitus, since Progenitus goes into its owner's library).

Why: Pain makes Nico discard a card. Progenitus's own ability says "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." So instead of going to the graveyard, Progenitus is revealed and shuffled into its owner's library. That shuffle is caused by an ability (Progenitus's replacement ability), which is exactly what Psychogenic Probe watches for: "Whenever a spell or ability causes a player to shuffle their library, this artifact deals 2 damage to that player." The damage goes to the player who shuffled, not to Amare, even though Amare controls Psychogenic Probe. Note that Progenitus's protection from everything doesn't matter here — Psychogenic Probe damages a player, not Progenitus, and Pain targets a player rather than Progenitus.

Also worth noting: Psychogenic Probe's trigger doesn't depend on the library's contents — it triggers even if the shuffling player's library is empty. If instead Nico discarded a card that was not Progenitus (or a different owner's Progenitus were involved), the 2 damage would go to whoever actually shuffled. This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the trigger simply hits whichever player performed the shuffle.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Progenitus's replacement effect changes the effect of Pain from "Nico discards a card, putting it into their graveyard" to "Nico reveals a card and shuffles it into their library". Pain still caused the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers.

entries.question: Albert controls [Doubling Season] and [Pir, Imaginative Rascal] and activates the +1 ability of [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes]. How many loyalty counters does it gain?
entries.reason: The candidate says Ajani gains only 1 loyalty counter, but the reference says it gains 4 because Pir replaces the single counter with two and Doubling Season then doubles those, yielding four.
entries.answer:
Ajani, Mentor of Heroes gains exactly 1 loyalty counter — neither Doubling Season nor Pir, Imaginative Rascal increases it.

Why: the "+1" in a planeswalker's ability is a cost you pay as you activate the ability, not something an effect does. Doubling Season's ruling states this explicitly: "if you activate an ability whose cost has you put loyalty counters on a planeswalker, the number you put on isn't doubled. This is because those counters are put on as a cost, not as an effect" [Doubling Season ruling #4]. Doubling Season only replaces counters an *effect* would put on a permanent you control, and Pir, Imaginative Rascal likewise replaces counters that "would be put on a permanent your team controls" by an effect — the rulings for Pir, Imaginative Rascal describe it applying to counter-placing instructions from effects and to permanents entering with counters [Pir, Imaginative Rascal ruling #4] [Pir, Imaginative Rascal ruling #5], not to cost payments.

Secondary note (the part that *is* boosted): when the first +1 ability of Ajani, Mentor of Heroes resolves, the three +1/+1 counters it distributes are placed by an effect, so both Doubling Season and Pir, Imaginative Rascal apply to the counters going on each target creature. You still announce the distribution of the three counters (each target getting at least one) when activating [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes ruling #1].

This interaction doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Four.

Activating a planeswalker ability includes paying the loyalty cost, which in this case means adding one loyalty counter. Doubling Season only replaces effects, which are the result of a spell or ability. However Pir, Imaginative Rascal replaces the original one loyalty counter with two, which Doubling Season can then replace with doubling the additional loyalty counters, resulting in a total of four.

entries.question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly asserts Domestication can enchant a creature entering simultaneously and thus control its ETB, whereas the reference states that's impossible—the Aura must target an existing permanent.
entries.answer:
Nico controls Haru-Onna's enters-the-battlefield trigger, so Nico draws the card.

Why: with Show and Tell, all chosen cards are put onto the battlefield simultaneously (Aminah, as the player resolving/active player, chooses first, then Nico), and any choices those cards require — such as what Domestication enchants — are made after all players have chosen their card [Show and Tell ruling #0] [Show and Tell ruling #2]. So Haru-Onna and Domestication (already attached to Haru-Onna) hit the battlefield at the same moment.

Domestication's static ability says "You control enchanted creature," and that continuous effect is in place from the instant it enters. When the game looks at the resulting state to put Haru-Onna's "When this creature enters, draw a card" trigger on the stack, Nico is Haru-Onna's controller, so the trigger is controlled by Nico and Nico is the one who draws. Note Domestication's own end-step sacrifice trigger checks Haru-Onna's power (2), so it won't even trigger at 3 or less [Domestication ruling #0].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming both cards were put onto the battlefield by the same Show and Tell resolution, which is what makes them simultaneous. If instead Domestication somehow arrived after Haru-Onna was already on the battlefield, Aminah would have controlled the enters trigger and drawn the card, and only afterward would Nico gain control of Haru-Onna.

Multiplayer: the same result holds regardless of table size; if there are more players, each other player chooses their card in turn order after Aminah, and each ETB trigger is controlled by whoever controls that permanent once all the cards (and Auras' attachments) are in place [Show and Tell ruling #2].

Caveat: the numbered rules supplied here don't include the general trigger-controller or control-change rules; the conclusion rests on Domestication's printed "You control enchanted creature" plus the Show and Tell rulings on simultaneity.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nico must choose a permanent that is already on the battlefield for the Domestication to enchant. They can't choose a permanent that is entering at the same time.

entries.question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Fatal Push can target Skyhunter Patrol (mana value doesn't matter when targeting) and that Founding the Third Path is sacrificed as the ability finishes resolving, satisfying revolt so Fatal Push will destroy Skyhunter Patrol.
entries.answer:
Yes, Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, and by the time the Fatal Push copy resolves Skyhunter Patrol will most likely be destroyed — because Founding the Third Path gets sacrificed in between, which turns on revolt.

Targeting: Fatal Push may target any creature regardless of mana value; its mana value is checked only on resolution [Fatal Push ruling #3]. Skyhunter Patrol is a legal target even though its mana value is 4.

Casting: Founding the Third Path's chapter III exiles the instant or sorcery card from the graveyard, copies it, and lets Amani cast the copy — but Amani must pay all costs for that copy, here {B} (one black mana), and must cast it immediately as the ability resolves [Founding the Third Path ruling #2].

Why Skyhunter Patrol dies: Founding the Third Path's read ahead text says "Sacrifice after III." So once the chapter III ability finishes resolving, Founding the Third Path is sacrificed and leaves the battlefield under Amani's control. That happens before the newly cast Fatal Push copy resolves (the copy is put on the stack during chapter III's resolution and resolves later). Revolt only asks whether a permanent left the battlefield under your control this turn — it doesn't care why, who caused it, or where it went, and a sacrificed permanent counts [Fatal Push ruling #2]. So when Fatal Push resolves, revolt is satisfied and it destroys Skyhunter Patrol because its mana value (4) is 4 or less.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the standard sequence — chapter III resolves, Fatal Push is cast during that resolution, Founding the Third Path is then sacrificed, and Fatal Push resolves afterward. If instead you evaluate the moment Fatal Push is cast (or if some effect kept Founding the Third Path on the battlefield, e.g. its chapter number was such that it isn't sacrificed, or another effect saved it), revolt would not be satisfied and Fatal Push would do nothing to Skyhunter Patrol, since 4 is greater than 2. Note that revolt is checked only on resolution, not on casting.

Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, and the provided rules include no multiplayer-specific wrinkle for it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, and it will be destroyed by Fatal Push.

Fatal Push does not check for the target's mana value when put on the stack, so Amani is allowed to target Skyhunter Patrol.

Amani will put Fatal Push on the stack as part of the resolution of Founding the Third Path's third chapter. Once the ability is done resolving, SBAs are checked and the saga is sacrificed. In particular this means that Amani will have Revolt when Fatal Push resolves, thus Skyhunter Patrol will get destroyed.

entries.question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
entries.reason: Both conclude Titania's Song makes Soldevi Digger a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities and that Bludgeon Brawl no longer applies once it is a creature.
entries.answer:
Soldevi Digger becomes a 2/2 artifact creature named Soldevi Digger with no abilities, and it is no longer an Equipment.

Why:
- Titania's Song reads "Each noncreature artifact loses all abilities and becomes an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value." Soldevi Digger is a noncreature artifact when Titania's Song resolves, so it becomes an artifact creature, and its mana value is {2} (mana value 2), making it 2/2. It loses its "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library" ability.
- Bludgeon Brawl only affects "each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact." Once Soldevi Digger is a creature, Bludgeon Brawl's effect no longer applies to it: it stops being an Equipment and loses the granted equip {X} and "Equipped creature gets +X/+0" ability, and it becomes unattached from any creature it was attached to while remaining on the battlefield [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2]. (Consistently, an Equipment that's also a creature can't be equipped to anything [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #3].)
- So the final characteristics: name Soldevi Digger, card types Artifact Creature, no subtypes granted by Bludgeon Brawl, no abilities, power and toughness 2/2, mana cost {2} (colorless), mana value 2.

Two practical notes: Soldevi Digger can attack or use {T} abilities only if Ari has continuously controlled it since the beginning of their most recent turn, regardless of how long it has been a creature [Titania's Song ruling #0] — though here it has no abilities left to tap for. And if Titania's Song later leaves the battlefield, its own text says the effect continues until end of turn; only after that does Soldevi Digger stop being a creature and again fall under Bludgeon Brawl as an Equipment.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities. Applying Titania's Song would cause Bludgeon Brawl to no longer apply (since Soldevi Digger would be a creature). However, applying Bludgeon Brawl would not change how Titania's Song's effect is applied, so Bludgeon Brawl is dependent on Titania's Song. Titania's Song applies first, and then Bludgeon Brawl won't affect Soldevi Digger since it's a creature.

entries.question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the same outcome: Enlarge ends leaving -1/-1 counters that kill Goblin Piker, and Baron Sengir (having dealt infect damage) survives and gets the trigger/+2/+2 counter.
entries.answer:
At end of turn Goblin Piker dies, and Baron Sengir survives and grows.

Step by step, assuming combat damage was dealt normally in the combat damage step:

1. Enlarge makes Goblin Piker 9/8 with trample until end of turn. Grafted Exoskeleton makes Baron Sengir 7/7 with infect, and Withstand Death makes Baron Sengir indestructible until end of turn.
2. Goblin Piker (9/8 trample) assigns lethal damage to Baron Sengir (7) and may assign the remaining 2 to Nico via trample. Indestructible doesn't change how much damage counts as lethal for assignment. That 7 damage is marked on Baron Sengir but Withstand Death's indestructible means damage won't destroy it, so Baron Sengir survives.
3. Baron Sengir deals 7 damage to Goblin Piker, but because of Grafted Exoskeleton's infect, that damage is dealt as seven -1/-1 counters instead. Infect damage is still damage in all respects [Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #2]. Goblin Piker is 9/8, so with seven -1/-1 counters it's a 2/1 and survives combat. Those -1/-1 counters stay on it permanently — they don't wear off at end of turn [Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #6].
4. When the turn ends, Enlarge's "+7/+7 until end of turn" wears off in the cleanup step. Goblin Piker goes back to base 2/1 but still has the seven -1/-1 counters, making it -5/-6. Its toughness is 0 or less, so it dies immediately as a state-based action (indestructible wouldn't have saved it either, per Withstand Death's own reminder text about 0-or-less toughness).
5. Goblin Piker was dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn (infect damage is damage), so Baron Sengir's triggered ability triggers when Goblin Piker dies, and a +2/+2 counter is put on Baron Sengir. Baron Sengir's marked damage also wears off during that cleanup step, and Withstand Death's indestructible ends, but Baron Sengir has no damage left on it and remains on the battlefield, now larger.

Timing note: I assumed damage was dealt in the normal combat damage step with all three effects (Enlarge, Grafted Exoskeleton, Withstand Death) already applying. If Withstand Death had been cast after combat damage, Baron Sengir would have been destroyed by 7 damage before end of turn instead, and only Goblin Piker's end-of-turn death would remain (with no Baron Sengir around to get a counter). Nothing here depends on the player count: with more than two players the only difference is that the trample damage goes to whichever player or planeswalker Goblin Piker was attacking.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Enlarge wears off, but the -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker remain. Goblin Piker dies. It was dealt damage that turn by Baron Sengir, so Baron Sengir triggers.

entries.question: Niko has a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] in their graveyard with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ashley controls [Containment Priest], and casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Niko. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Containment Priest causes Skullbriar to be exiled instead of entering the battlefield and that its +1/+1 counters remain with it in exile.
entries.answer:
Ashley's Ghastly Conscription resolves, but every card it would manifest ends up exiled by Containment Priest instead — including Niko's Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. Nothing enters the battlefield for Ashley.

Step by step:

1. Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from Niko's graveyard in a face-down pile, shuffles that pile, then manifests those cards — Ashley would put them onto the battlefield face down as 2/2 creatures under Ashley's control.
2. A manifested permanent is a 2/2 creature with no name, mana cost, creature types, or abilities [Ghastly Conscription ruling #8]. So each card is a nontoken creature that would enter the battlefield without having been cast — exactly what Containment Priest replaces: "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead." Manifesting is not casting, so Containment Priest applies. (Compare [Containment Priest ruling #3]: what matters is whether the object is a creature as it enters, which a manifested card is.)
3. Therefore Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and every other creature card from Niko's graveyard are exiled rather than put onto the battlefield. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave never becomes a face-down 2/2 on the battlefield, so Ashley never gets the option to turn it face up for its mana cost {B}{G} [Ghastly Conscription ruling #2].
4. Counters: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's third ability ("Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library") works only if it has that ability in the zone it's moving from [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1], and it applies to all counter kinds [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5]. It had that ability in Niko's graveyard, so the 2 +1/+1 counters stay with it as it goes to exile, and it's a 2/2 in exile [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2]. Note that once it left the graveyard it became a new object with no relation to its previous existence [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #3]; while face down it has no abilities, so the counters won't survive a further zone change unless it has the ability in the zone it next moves from.
5. Ownership is unchanged: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave sits in exile as a card Niko owns.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Containment Priest is already on the battlefield when Ghastly Conscription resolves (as stated). If Containment Priest instead entered or was flashed in after the manifest had already happened, the manifested creatures would already be on the battlefield and would not be exiled — Containment Priest only replaces entry events that occur while it's on the battlefield.

Player count doesn't matter here: Ghastly Conscription targets one player (Niko), and Containment Priest's replacement effect applies to any nontoken creature entering. The provided rules add nothing that changes this between a two-player game and a larger table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: In order for counters to remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, it needs to have that ability immediately before it changes zones. It did have that ability in the graveyard, so it is exiled face down with the +1/+1 counters remaining on it during that change. It then attempts to enter the battlefield, but remains in exile instead due to Containment Priest. Since it becomes a new object, it will be face-up in exile. However it didn't change zones, so the counters will remain on it in exile.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
entries.reason: The candidate states Ashley cannot activate it again because the once-per-turn restriction persists, but the reference says the card stopped being revealed and became a new object so Skill Borrower gains a new ability and can be activated again.
entries.answer:
No — Ashley can't activate the Putrid Leech ability a second time this turn. Putrid Leech's own text says "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn. Activate only once each turn." That restriction is part of the ability Skill Borrower gains, so it limits Skill Borrower to one activation of that ability per turn; shuffling Putrid Leech off the top and back on top doesn't reset it, because the limit is on activating the ability during the turn, not on how long Skill Borrower has had it. Printed card text like "Activate only once each turn" governs here.

Details and assumptions:
- Skill Borrower has all activated abilities of the top card of Ashley's library while that card is an artifact or creature card, so with Putrid Leech on top it has "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn. Activate only once each turn" (paying 2 life is a cost, and the colon marks it as an activated ability) [Skill Borrower ruling #2].
- The first activation resolved (or at least was activated) legally. Note that if the top card had changed while Ashley was in the middle of activating it, the ability would still be activated and resolve normally even though Skill Borrower lost it [Skill Borrower ruling #4] — so the activation still "counts" for the once-per-turn limit.
- The +2/+2 is a modification, not a set value, so it applies in layer 7c and makes Skill Borrower 3/5 until end of turn [613.4c].
- Sensei's Divining Top's first ability ({1}: look at top three, put back in any order) only rearranges the library; it doesn't reset any activation limits [Sensei's Divining Top ruling #0].
- Timing note: I'm assuming Ashley activated the Putrid Leech ability via Skill Borrower before manipulating the library. If instead Ashley never actually activated it (e.g., only intended to), then once Putrid Leech is back on top Ashley may activate it for the first time this turn normally.
- Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Putrid Leech stopped being revealed for a time, so it is no longer the same object that it was before. Skill Borrower has a new ability that just has the same text as the ability that was activated earlier.

entries.question: Noah controls a [Mons's Goblin Raiders] enchanted with a [Spider Umbra]. Alexandra casts [Yamabushi's Flame], targeting Mons's Goblin Raiders. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Spider Umbra is destroyed, Mons's Goblin Raiders survives (is not exiled), and Yamabushi's Flame's replacement only applies later if the creature would die that turn.
entries.answer:
Mons's Goblin Raiders survives. Spider Umbra is destroyed instead, and Mons's Goblin Raiders is not exiled.

Details:
- With Spider Umbra attached, Mons's Goblin Raiders is a 2/2 (1/1 plus +1/+1). Yamabushi's Flame deals 3 damage to it, which is lethal damage, so Mons's Goblin Raiders would be destroyed.
- Umbra armor (the ability on Spider Umbra) is a mandatory replacement: instead of Mons's Goblin Raiders being destroyed, all damage is removed from Mons's Goblin Raiders and Spider Umbra is destroyed [Spider Umbra ruling #4], [Spider Umbra ruling #6]. Here it's the game's lethal-damage rules, not Yamabushi's Flame itself, that cause Spider Umbra to be destroyed [Spider Umbra ruling #0].
- Because Mons's Goblin Raiders never dies, Yamabushi's Flame's exile clause ("If a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead") never applies to it. Note that clause remains active for the rest of the turn: if Mons's Goblin Raiders would die later this turn (and no other umbra armor Aura saves it), it is exiled instead.
- Afterward Mons's Goblin Raiders is back to 1/1 with no damage marked on it, since umbra armor removed all damage. Umbra armor is not regeneration, so Mons's Goblin Raiders is not tapped and isn't removed from combat [Spider Umbra ruling #3].
- If Mons's Goblin Raiders somehow had indestructible, umbra armor would do nothing because the damage simply wouldn't destroy it, and Spider Umbra would stay [Spider Umbra ruling #2].

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Spider Umbra is destroyed and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield.

There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the same event. Umbra armor is attempting to replace the destruction of the creature, while Yamabushi's Flame's effect is attempting to replace where the creature moves to. The "move to the graveyard" event is a part of the "destroy" event, so the umbra armor replacement effect must apply first. Once that effect has been applied, the creature is no longer about to die, so there are no more effects to apply.

If the Mons's Goblin Raiders would die later in the turn, the Yamabushi's Flame's replacement effect will apply at that time and cause it to move to exile instead of the graveyard.

entries.question: At the beginning of the game, Alex announced [Kaheera, the Orphanguard] as their companion. During the game, Alex cast [Carrion Grub] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alex restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Alex can re-announce Kaheera (treating Carrion Grub as not violating the companion restriction), while the reference states Carrion Grub ends up in the shuffled library and therefore prevents Kaheera from being announced.
entries.answer:
Short answer: the restart begins a brand-new game, so Alex gets to go through the pregame procedure again — including revealing Kaheera, the Orphanguard as a companion once more — and the {3} companion special action is available again because it's "once per game" and this is a new game. Carrion Grub, which Alex brought in from outside the game with Wish, is not one of the cards that stays in exile, so it doesn't come back onto the battlefield with Karn Liberated's ability.

Details:

1. Restarting ends the old game entirely. Karn Liberated's −14 immediately ends the preceding game with no winner or loser, and the players immediately begin a new one [Karn Liberated ruling #12]. Nothing that happened in the old game carries over [Karn Liberated ruling #1]. Each player shuffles their deck, resets to the starting life total, draws seven, and may mulligan; Karn Liberated's controller (Alex) is the starting player [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. Players may not move cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #5].

2. Kaheera, the Orphanguard can be announced again. Companions are revealed as part of the pregame procedure, before shuffling, with the starting player revealing first and then in turn order [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #0, Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #3]. Since the new game has its own pregame procedure, Alex may again reveal Kaheera, the Orphanguard from outside the game, and the once-per-game {3} special action to put it into hand is likewise fresh [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #14, Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #5]. Note the companion requirement checks only Alex's starting deck, not the sideboard [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #2] — so Carrion Grub (an Insect) sitting in the sideboard never broke the requirement and doesn't now.

3. Carrion Grub. Only non-Aura permanent cards that were exiled by Karn Liberated's +4 or −3 abilities stay in exile and are put onto the battlefield under Alex's control after the restart; those pairs of abilities are linked [Karn Liberated ruling #6, Karn Liberated ruling #4]. Carrion Grub was cast off Wish, not exiled with Karn Liberated, so it isn't among those cards and gets no special treatment. Once played from outside the game it was simply a card in the game like any other [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #11, Wish ruling #0], and the new game is set up fresh with each player's deck and sideboard as they were, since cards can't be shifted between them [Karn Liberated ruling #5]. The provided material doesn't spell out the exact zone Carrion Grub ends up in for the new game beyond that; if Alex still wants it, Alex would need another Wish-style effect. (If, alternatively, Karn Liberated had exiled Carrion Grub with +4 or −3 before the restart, it would remain in exile and be put onto the battlefield under Alex's control, having been continuously controlled since the start of Alex's first turn — able to attack and use {T} abilities [Karn Liberated ruling #2].)

4. Table size: with exactly two players, the above is all that applies. At a multiplayer table, any player who had already left the game before the restart is not part of the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #11], and companion reveals proceed from the starting player in turn order [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #3].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Carrion Grub will be shuffled into Alex's library along with the rest of the cards in the game. Because Carrion Grub violates Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion restriction, Alex can't announce it as their companion for the restarted game.
